messages.content: Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6.

function.name: statistics_calculate_p_value
function.description: Calculate the p-value for a t-test on a single sample from a population. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

sample_mean.description: The mean of the sample data. This is a float type value.

population_mean.description: The mean of the population data. This is a float type value.

sample_std_dev.description: The standard deviation of the sample data. This is a float type value.

sample_size.description: The size of the sample data.

two_tailed.description: Whether the test is two-tailed. If not provided, default is true.

message.content:
**Standard error (the “standard deviation” of the sampling distribution of the mean)**  

\[
SE=\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}=\frac{1.4}{\sqrt{40}}\approx\frac{1.4}{6.3249}\approx0.2215
\]

So the standard deviation of the null‑hypothesis sampling distribution of the sample mean is **≈ 0.22**.
message.reasoning:
The user says: "Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6." They want the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test? That might refer to the standard error of the mean under the null hypothesis? Usually we compute the standard error as sample_std_dev / sqrt(sample_size). But they mention "standard deviation of the null hypothesis test" which could be the standard error of the sampling distribution of the sample mean under the null. So we compute SE = sample_std_dev / sqrt(sample_size) = 1.4 / sqrt(40). sqrt(40) ~ 6.3249. So SE ≈ 1.4 / 6.3249 ≈ 0.2215. So the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean (under the null) is about 0.2215.

But maybe they want the standard deviation of the null distribution of the test statistic? For a t-test, the test statistic t = (sample_mean - population_mean) / (sample_std_dev / sqrt(sample_size)). The denominator is the standard error. So the standard deviation of the null distribution of the test statistic is 1 (for t distribution with df=39). But they ask "Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test". That phrase is ambiguous. But likely they want the standard error of the mean. So answer: 0.2215.

We can also compute the t-statistic: t = (98.2 - 98.6) / (1.4 / sqrt(40)) = (-0.4) / 0.2215 = -1.805. But they didn't ask for t. They asked for standard deviation. So answer: 0.2215.

We should provide the calculation steps. Also note that the standard deviation of the null distribution of the sample mean is the standard error. So answer: approximately 0.2215.

We can also mention that if they want the standard deviation of the t distribution, it's sqrt(df/(df-2)) for df>2. For df=39, that's sqrt(39/37) ≈ sqrt(1.05405) ≈ 1.0268. But likely they want the standard error.

Thus answer: 0.2215.
